headline: Of 464 Rust programs generated from 116 buggy C programs by four automated refactoring tools, 413 compile, 177 still carry the original memory-safety bug, and 77 have a new one.

items.title: Transport says the niobium film is fine; the resonator says otherwise
items.dek: J. T. Paustian and eight co-authors at Syracuse, Cornell and Wisconsin–Madison sputtered niobium films spanning an 840-megapascal range of built-in stress, measured the same superconducting transition temperature of about 9.0 kelvin in all of them, and then found microwave losses implying a second superconducting gap that closes near 2.4 kelvin.
items.why_it_matters: Two acceptance tests for the same deposition disagree, and the cheap one is the blind one. Transition temperature and residual resistance ratio from a four-point probe are what most labs use to sign off a superconducting film, and across this stress range neither of them moves at all while the microwave loss changes by orders of magnitude. If the low-gap population is a stress-nucleated second crystalline phase, then qualifying a sputter recipe means measuring film stress and building a resonator, and the answer is not simply the least-stressed film: the best resonators here came from the middle of the range, at −371 megapascals.
items.background_md: A superconductor carries microwave current almost without loss only while the excitations that can absorb energy stay rare, and how rare is set by the energy gap Δ: their number falls off as exp(−Δ/k_BT), so a small-gap region inside an otherwise good film dissipates far more than its volume fraction suggests. A 5 gigahertz photon carries about 20 microelectronvolts, well below niobium's pair-breaking threshold, so the drive itself breaks no pairs and the loss reports only the thermal population already there. Sputtered films also arrive with biaxial stress locked in, set by how much momentum the depositing atoms retain — a knob on the tool, not a property of the metal.
items.deeper_md:
Stress was set with three knobs on an AJA Orion 5 sputter tool — argon pressure, target-to-substrate throw distance, and deposition time — across eleven recipes; five went into resonators at 60–65 nm thickness, at −737 ± 72, −542 ± 56, −371 ± 33, −56 ± 47 and +100 ± 77 MPa, negative being compressive. Transport gave T_c = 9.0 ± 0.2 K and residual resistance ratio 4.0 ± 0.6 with no correlation to stress at all.

Each chip carries eight quarter-wave coplanar-waveguide resonators, 6 µm centre trace and 3 µm gap, covering 4.2–6.3 GHz. Fitting the temperature dependence of loss and frequency shift with a single-phase Mattis–Bardeen conductivity returns an effective T_c of 2.4 ± 0.2 K, roughly a quarter of the transport value; the −737 MPa film reaches a loss of order 10⁻⁵, while the −371 MPa film gives the best resonators of the set.

The candidate is ω-phase niobium, a hexagonal variant Lee and colleagues found in about 1 vol.% of grains in stressed HiPIMS films, in patches 10–100 nm across; its predicted transition temperature is about 2.3 K. The authors are careful that their data cannot fix the origin, spatial distribution or volume fraction of the low-gap regions, that the fitted amplitudes are effective weights rather than phase fractions, and that an inhomogeneous gap landscape would look much the same.

glossary.definition: Resistance at room temperature divided by resistance just above the superconducting transition; it measures how much electron scattering comes from defects and impurities rather than from lattice vibrations.
The in-plane force per unit cross-section locked into a deposited film. Compressive, written negative, means the film would expand if released, and it bows the wafer it sits on.
The fraction of a resonator's stored electromagnetic energy dissipated per radian of oscillation; a loss of order 10⁻⁵ means the resonator rings about 100,000 radians before decaying.
The BCS prediction for a superconductor's complex conductivity at microwave frequencies. Fitting it to measured loss and frequency shift is how a gap is extracted from a resonator.

items.fab_angle: Argon pressure and throw distance are the two settings on a teaching-lab sputterer a student is most likely to change casually, and this paper is a direct map from them onto film stress. You do not need a dilution refrigerator to walk the first half of it: deposit the same film at two pressures, measure wafer curvature before and after on the profilometer, and Stoney's equation turns the change into a stress number you can put on the recipe sheet.

items.title: Harmonic acoustic resonances, and 33 of 36 devices land in tolerance
items.dek: Sandia National Laboratories built silicon-nitride waveguides that carry their own gigahertz sound waves — acousto-optic modulators, which shift a light beam's frequency by the acoustic frequency — with two resonances placed an octave apart at 1.14 and 2.28 gigahertz, and 33 of 36 devices across three 200-millimetre wafers met the alignment tolerance with no tuning.
items.why_it_matters: A single acoustic tone can only move light onto one sideband, and the arithmetic of sinusoidal phase modulation caps how much power lands there at about a third. Driving two harmonically related tones through the same released beam shapes the phase in time rather than merely wiggling it, which is how the single-sideband figure reaches half and how a flat seven-line comb becomes available from one device. The yield number is the harder claim: matching two mechanical resonances to a fixed ratio normally needs per-device trimming, and a foundry process that lands them in tolerance across wafers is the difference between a laboratory demonstration and something an atomic clock or ion trap can specify.
items.background_md: Light and sound interact inside a solid because strain changes the refractive index — the photoelastic effect. Send an acoustic wave along a waveguide and it modulates the optical phase at the acoustic frequency, scattering power out of the carrier into sidebands offset by exactly that frequency; unlike an electro-optic modulator, the shift is set by a mechanical resonance rather than by a voltage. Atomic physics is why anyone wants this on a chip: the transitions used in clocks, ion traps and cold-atom experiments sit at visible wavelengths and need offsets of order a gigahertz, which bulk crystals deliver bulkily and most integrated modulators cannot deliver at visible wavelengths without heavy loss.
items.deeper_md:
The stack is a 300 nm silicon-nitride core with 690 nm of oxide above and 710 nm below, capped with aluminium nitride and electrodes, released into a 1.4 µm-wide beam with 5 µm trenches either side; the SiN core inside is 1.1 µm wide and each section is roughly 5 µm × 2 mm. Two breathing modes were designed at 1.14 GHz and 2.28 GHz, with measured linewidths averaging 16.5 MHz and 24.4 MHz across 36 devices and half-wave voltages of V_π,1 = 2.87 V and V_π,2 = 1.49 V. At 730 nm the device reaches 50% single-sideband conversion against a 33.9% single-tone limit, 60 dB carrier suppression with 53 dB image suppression simultaneously, and a seven-line comb holding 92% of the optical power within 2 dB peak to peak.

Two caveats. Insertion loss on the representative device is 17.7 dB, which the authors attribute mostly to grating couplers rather than to propagation — the same group's low-confinement version of this platform runs 2.6 dB/m at 780 nm, so the figure is a packaging artefact rather than a material one. And the mechanical quality factor that makes the resonant enhancement possible also sets the response time: 102 ns and 95 ns rise times for the two modes. This is a frequency-agile device, not a fast switch.

glossary.definition: A device in which a travelling acoustic wave strains a medium and so modulates its refractive index, scattering light into sidebands offset from the carrier by exactly the acoustic frequency.
The drive voltage producing π radians of optical phase shift — the standard measure of how hard a modulator is to drive. Here 1.49 V and 2.87 V for the two acoustic modes.
The fraction of input optical power that ends up in one chosen frequency-shifted output. A single sinusoidal tone caps it near 34%, which is the reason to add a second harmonic.
A mechanical resonance in which a released structure expands and contracts across its width, so the strain it generates overlaps the optical mode confined in the same beam.

items.fab_angle: The released beam and its 5 µm isolation trenches are a MEMS release process sitting on top of a photonic one, and the quantity that has to be uniform is not a linewidth but a frequency ratio — two mechanical modes at exactly 2:1, which depends on the beam width and the film thicknesses together. That is a case where ellipsometry or scatterometry on the deposited stack predicts device yield more directly than a critical-dimension measurement does.

items.title: 512 gigabytes of on-package flash, and 25 microseconds to reach it
items.dek: Jongjin Baek and three co-authors, writing in IEEE Computer Architecture Letters, simulate an accelerator package that pairs high-bandwidth memory with high-bandwidth flash — stacked 3D NAND on the same package, about 512 gigabytes per stack at read bandwidth comparable to HBM4 — and hold 3,900 idle agent sessions resident instead of 165.
items.why_it_matters: Flash read bandwidth is close to HBM's; flash read latency is four orders of magnitude worse, and its write endurance is finite. That combination makes the tier useless as memory and useful as a place to park state that is cold but must not be recomputed, which is exactly what a multi-turn agent's key-value cache is between tool calls. The design consequence is that the eviction policy stops being a performance detail and becomes a wear-out budget: writing every cache block to flash rather than only the evicted ones costs about 950 watts per device at 20 picojoules per bit, and spends program/erase cycles on blocks that were about to be read again anyway.
items.background_md: A transformer serving a conversation keeps a key-value cache — the per-token intermediate state that lets it attend to everything already said without recomputing it. The cache grows linearly with context and belongs to one session, so a server holding many idle sessions runs out of memory capacity long before it runs out of arithmetic. High-bandwidth memory answers the bandwidth half of that by stacking DRAM dies on the accelerator package and wiring them with thousands of through-silicon vias, but capacity per stack is limited by the area of a DRAM storage capacitor, which is the part of the memory that has scaled worst.
items.deeper_md:
The assumed flash stack holds roughly 512 GB against 48–64 GB for an HBM4 stack, reads at 1,638 GB/s, has 25 µs read access latency, costs 8–30 pJ/bit to read against about 3.5 pJ/bit for HBM, and survives 100,000 program/erase cycles. Baseline is a B200 with 192 GiB of HBM3e at 8 TB/s and 2.25 PFLOP/s, serving Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B — 56.8 GiB of BF16 weights and 96 KiB of KV per token, so a 16.7k-token session is 1.53 GiB. The policy is write-on-evict with least-recently-used ordering at 1.5 MiB block granularity; time between tokens is 14 ms at 48 active sessions and 27 ms at 128, while resident sessions rise from 165 to 3,900 with a 3 TiB flash tier.

All of it is a trace-driven simulator with analytical latency and power models, fed by mini-swe-agent trajectories on SWE-bench Verified — there is no HBF part to measure. The endurance assumption is the weak point: SanDisk and SK hynix have taken the format to the Open Compute Project rather than JEDEC, and Semiconductor Engineering's reporting on the same technology notes commodity NAND endurance sits in the thousands of cycles, with 100,000 rare. At Hot Chips 2026 the presenters said plainly that no HBF products exist yet, and that the format wins on cost per capacity and loses on cost per bandwidth.

glossary.definition: The keys and values a transformer has already computed for earlier tokens. Keeping them turns attention over a long context from repeated computation into a lookup, at the cost of memory that grows with every token.
Picojoules to read or move one bit. Multiplying it by terabytes per second gives watts, which is why it decides whether a memory tier is thermally affordable at all.
One write-and-wipe of a NAND block. Flash cells tolerate a finite number before the tunnel oxide degrades, so any flash tier's lifetime is a function of how often software writes to it.
A tiering policy that copies a block down to the slower tier only when it is pushed out of the faster one, so blocks that are re-read while still resident never cost a flash write.

items.title: A load/store bus instead of Ethernet, across host boundaries
items.dek: IEIT SYSTEMS describes Co-Fabric, a four-layer bus that gives 64 accelerators one shared memory address space across eight separate host machines, and reports inter-node latency at 10 to 20 percent of a remote-direct-memory-access-over-Ethernet baseline on the same 3D-mesh wiring.
items.why_it_matters: Scale-up interconnect is currently a choice between two compromises: a network stack that has to be told which host owns which memory, or a host bus that cannot leave the chassis. Extending load, store and atomic semantics across host domains takes the message-passing layer out of the accelerator's critical path, which is where the latency claim comes from — the fabric layer routes on a port identifier carried in the packet header rather than on a per-host address. It also relocates the failure question: one address space across eight machines means a fault in one node can now reach another node's memory, and nothing in the paper says what stops it.
items.background_md: Scale-up and scale-out are different problems. Inside a small group of accelerators a model's tensors are split so finely that every layer needs a collective operation, so the interconnect's latency and its semantics matter more than its reach: a load instruction that lands in another chip's memory is cheaper than a message the receiving side has to interpret. Ethernet-based remote direct memory access was built for scale-out and carries a message abstraction and per-host addressing with it; PCIe-style buses have load/store semantics but stop at the edge of one machine's address space. Work in this area is mostly an attempt to get one property without paying for the other.
items.deeper_md:
The stack is media, link, fabric and semantic layers: credit-based flow control and link-level retransmission below, port-ID routing and global address mapping in the middle, native load/store and atomics on top, with shadow-device auto-enumeration assembling the unified address space. Ports are ×16 at 32 Gb/s per lane, so 512 Gb/s per accelerator. The demonstrated system is 64 accelerators — eight nodes of eight, full mesh inside a node and rail-only across nodes, over direct-attach copper in a two-cabinet build. Reported latency is 10–20% of the RoCE baseline below 4 MB messages and 15–50% from 4 to 64 MB; AllGather falls from about 80 s to about 20 s, and DeepSeek R1 inference improves by 30–80%.

Read the two cost numbers together. Replacing Ethernet NICs and switches with retimers and Co-Fabric switches is claimed to cut interconnect cost about 80% but interconnect power only about 5%, both from a bill-of-materials comparison rather than a model. No absolute latency in nanoseconds appears anywhere in the paper, so its "nanosecond-scale processing" is not checkable from the text. The competing answer is standardised rather than proprietary: UALink 200G 1.0 specifies 200 Gb/s per lane across up to 1,024 accelerators, six times this per-lane rate, and the Ultra Ethernet Consortium published version 1.0.3 in July 2026 arguing the same job can be done on Ethernet.

glossary.definition: Scale-up is the tightly coupled group of accelerators sharing one model's tensors, which needs microsecond collectives; scale-out is the looser network between such groups, where throughput matters more than latency.
An interconnect on which a processor reads remote memory with an ordinary memory instruction, so there is no message to build, send, or parse at either end of the link.
Remote direct memory access carried in Ethernet frames. It bypasses the remote CPU but keeps Ethernet's per-host addressing and its message-based operations.
The signalling rate on one differential pair. Aggregate link bandwidth is that rate times the lane count, so ×16 at 32 Gb/s is 512 Gb/s before encoding overhead.

items.title: Less unsafe Rust, same bug: 177 of 413 translations still fail
items.dek: Hung-Mao Chen and four co-authors ran four automated C-to-Rust refactoring tools over 116 C programs carrying known memory-safety bugs from NIST's Juliet test suite, and found that 177 of the 413 Rust programs that compiled still contain the original bug.
items.why_it_matters: The tools optimise a proxy. "Safety" in their objective means the fraction of the program sitting outside an unsafe block — C2SaferRust, for one, reports up to 38 percent fewer raw pointers and 28 percent less unsafe code — and that quantity can fall while the defect stays exactly where it was, because a null dereference or an out-of-bounds index expressed in safe Rust panics instead of corrupting memory and still stops the program. Anyone planning a migration on the strength of an unsafe-line count now has a measured gap between the metric and the outcome, plus 77 new bugs the tools introduced, 52 of them from a single tool.
items.background_md: Rust's guarantee is a compile-time one: the borrow checker proves that no two references mutate the same memory at once and that nothing outlives what it points at, and code that must break those rules has to be written inside an `unsafe` block. Automatic C-to-Rust translation starts from a transpiler that emits Rust which compiles and behaves identically but is almost entirely `unsafe`, because C pointer arithmetic has no safe equivalent. The research problem is rewriting that output into the safe subset without changing behaviour, and the field's usual scorecard for progress is how much `unsafe` is left.
items.deeper_md:
The corpus is 116 Juliet programs across five classes — 46 buffer overflow, 40 null-pointer dereference, 14 use-after-free, 12 double free, 4 type confusion — run through C2Rust-analyze, CROWN, C2SaferRust and a direct LLM translator, giving 464 outputs. Raw compile failures are 98, 116, 116 and 12; an LLM agent fixing trivial errors brings those to 29, 11, 11 and 0, leaving 413 compilable programs. Of those, 236 of the original defects are gone (57.1%), 177 programs still carry theirs, and 77 new bugs appear — 52 from C2Rust-analyze, 11 from CROWN, 8 from C2SaferRust, 6 from the LLM tool. New-bug categories include panics crossing a foreign-function-interface boundary and undefined behaviour inherited from the transpiler's own output.

The authors call their count a lower bound, and name the tooling gap that makes it one: AddressSanitizer does not flag Rust-specific undefined behaviour and Miri cannot execute across FFI boundaries, so no single detector covers all five classes. Juliet is also synthetic — small programs with one injected defect each and a fixed twin — so it measures refactoring behaviour rather than how these tools survive a real codebase's build system and macros. Nobody appears to dispute the direction of the result; the argument to expect is over whether Juliet's defect shapes are representative.

glossary.definition: A region of Rust where the compiler stops checking aliasing and lifetimes and the programmer accepts responsibility. How much of it remains is the usual, and here misleading, proxy for a translation's safety.
64,099 synthetic C/C++ programs spanning 118 CWE classes, published by the NSA's Center for Assured Software, each pairing a known injected defect with a fixed twin so a detector can be scored.
The boundary where Rust calls or is called by C. A Rust panic that unwinds across it is undefined behaviour, which is one way a rewrite counted as safe can still be unsound.
The paper's distinction: safety is the absence of unchecked memory operations, security the absence of an exploitable defect. A panic is safe and is still a denial of service.

items.title: A diffusion language model that drafts and verifies against itself
items.dek: MBZUAI's VILA Lab released Flash-dLLM, which speeds up LLaDA — an 8-billion-parameter language model that fills in masked tokens by denoising rather than predicting left to right — by 5.1× on the GSM8K arithmetic benchmark over the best previous cache method, with accuracy unchanged at 83.0 percent.
items.why_it_matters: Diffusion language models were supposed to win on parallelism and have been losing on memory traffic instead. Because any denoising step can rewrite any position, the standard key-value cache does not apply, and the workarounds recompute or re-materialise state until the arithmetic saving disappears into GPU memory bandwidth. Fusing the projection, the rotary embedding and the cache write into one kernel so intermediates never leave on-chip SRAM recovers 1.37× on its own; the rest comes from letting the model draft several tokens and check them against itself under a causal mask, which is speculative decoding without a second model to host.
items.background_md: An autoregressive language model emits one token at a time, each conditioned on the tokens before it, which is why its cached keys and values are never invalidated: token 40 cannot change what token 12 was. A masked diffusion language model instead starts from a sequence of mask symbols and repeatedly predicts all of them at once, unmasking the positions it is confident about and leaving the rest for the next pass. That buys parallelism — several tokens can settle per forward pass — at the price of the assumption that made caching free, because any position's representation can change on any step.
items.deeper_md:
The fused kernel performs the QKV projection, the rotary position embedding and the cache write in one CUDA launch, keeping intermediates in SRAM instead of round-tripping through HBM; measured alone on an RTX 3090 that is 1.37×. Flash-Verify then duplicates the search window into two views under a causal mask — one holding draft predictions, one still masked — accepts tokens in decoding order and discards everything after the first mismatch, so the model is its own drafter and verifier with no auxiliary network.

On LLaDA-1.5 at 512 tokens on one A100 80 GB: GSM8K 83.02% at 210.6 tokens/s against Elastic-Cache's 82.79% at 41.7 tokens/s, and HumanEval 40.24% at 185.6 tokens/s against 37.80% at 16.8 tokens/s. The repository quotes 22.3×–148.2× against greedy decoding with no cache at all, which is an honest measure of how bad the uncached baseline is rather than of how good this is.

Two limits the authors state: only masked diffusion models were tested, not continuous-space ones, and the benchmarks are structured-output tasks, so long-form generation — where accepting a whole drafted block is harder — is untested. Read the HumanEval figure as the model's rather than the method's: Flash-dLLM preserves accuracy, it does not raise it.

glossary.definition: One trained to recover tokens replaced by a mask symbol, generating text by repeatedly unmasking the positions it is most confident about instead of appending one token at a time.
Encoding a token's position by rotating its query and key vectors through an angle proportional to that position, so the attention score depends on the relative offset between tokens.
Merging several GPU operations into a single launch so intermediate arrays stay in on-chip SRAM. It helps precisely when the operations are limited by memory traffic rather than by arithmetic.
Guessing several tokens cheaply, then checking them in one pass of the expensive model and keeping the longest correct prefix — trading wasted work for fewer sequential steps.

foundations.topic: Bandgap references and analog first principles
foundations.subtitle: How to get a voltage that ignores temperature out of two transistors run at different current densities — and why the answer always lands near 1.2 volts.
foundations.tldr: Every analog circuit needs a voltage it can trust, and a transistor's base-emitter voltage is not it: it falls by roughly 2 millivolts for every kelvin. The bandgap reference gets around that by building a second voltage that rises with temperature — the difference between two base-emitter voltages at different current densities, which is exactly (kT/q)·ln(n) — and adding enough of it to cancel the first. What comes out sits near silicon's extrapolated bandgap, about 1.2 volts, and the whole craft of the field lives in the few parts per million per degree that refuse to cancel.

sections.heading: Nothing on a chip is a volt
sections.body_md: A CMOS process hands you three things you can trust and one you cannot. You can trust ratios: two capacitors laid out side by side match to about a tenth of a percent, and two resistors of the same material match nearly as well. You can trust that transistors of identical geometry behave identically, to within a mismatch that shrinks as you make them bigger. What you cannot trust is any absolute value. A polysilicon resistor's sheet resistance moves by tens of percent across process corners, a capacitor's absolute value moves with oxide thickness, and the supply rail is whatever the battery or the regulator upstream happens to be doing. Yet every analog-to-digital converter, every regulator, every temperature sensor and every current limit ultimately compares something against a voltage that is supposed to be a fixed number of volts. Building that number out of parts which individually do not know what a volt is — that is the problem this circuit exists to solve.

sections.heading: Two slopes, opposite signs
sections.body_md:
Start with the one quantity a silicon process reproduces well: the base-emitter voltage of a bipolar transistor at a known current. Analog Devices' courseware puts it near 650 millivolts at room temperature with a coefficient near −0.3 percent per degree, which is about −2 millivolts per kelvin. It falls with temperature because V_BE = V_T·ln(I_C/I_S) and the saturation current I_S climbs steeply, carrying a factor that goes as exp(−E_g/kT), so the logarithm shrinks faster than the thermal voltage V_T = kT/q grows.

Now run two transistors, or one transistor twice, at current densities differing by a factor n. The difference of the two base-emitter voltages is ΔV_BE = (kT/q)·ln(n) exactly — every process-dependent term cancels. Its slope is (k/q)·ln(n), and k/q is 0.0862 millivolts per kelvin, so a ratio of 8 gives 0.179 millivolts per kelvin. One slope is negative and made of material physics; the other is positive and made of nothing but two physical constants and a ratio you drew in layout.

sections.heading: Why the answer is the bandgap
sections.body_md: Add the two: V_REF = V_BE + G·ΔV_BE, and choose the gain G so the slopes cancel. With −2 millivolts per kelvin to kill and 0.179 available per unit of gain, G comes out near 11, and the output lands around 1.2 volts — which the same courseware notes is silicon's bandgap voltage, 1.205 volts. That is not a coincidence. Extrapolate V_BE back to absolute zero along its own linear term and it arrives at the bandgap, because the only thing holding a forward-biased junction's voltage up at 0 K is the energy it takes to make a carrier pair at all. Nulling the linear temperature term is the same operation as extrapolating to 0 K, so the reference voltage is forced towards the extrapolated bandgap no matter which transistor you used, what current you ran it at, or what ratio n you chose. The circuit is named after where the answer lands, not after how it works.

sections.heading: The part that will not cancel
sections.body_md:
The linear cancellation is not the end, because V_BE is not linear in temperature. The model used in the curvature-compensation literature is V_EB(T) = V_G0(T_r) − [V_G0(T_r) − V_EB0(T_r)]·(T/T_r) − V_T·(η−θ)·ln(T/T_r). The first term is a constant, the second is the straight ramp a PTAT voltage cancels exactly, and the third is a T·ln(T) term that it cannot, because no straight line cancels a curve. That leftover is called curvature, and it is what a reference's datasheet number is actually about.

The magnitudes are worth internalising. One 2022 curvature-compensated design reports that first-order compensation alone cannot get below roughly 13 parts per million per degree once that nonlinearity is present; its own untrimmed parts averaged 26.04 ppm/°C, and adding a curvature-correction term plus a per-part trim brought the best sample to 2.56 ppm/°C and the worst to 4.75 ppm/°C over −40 to +125 °C. That is a factor of ten in temperature coefficient bought with one extra current and a trim pass.

sections.heading: Offset, mismatch, and the zero-current trap
sections.body_md:
The gain of about 11 that makes the cancellation work also multiplies every error placed in front of it. An amplifier input offset of 1 millivolt appears at the output as roughly 11 millivolts on 1.2 volts — nearly one percent — and because offset itself drifts with temperature, it shows up in the specification as temperature coefficient rather than as plain inaccuracy. The same applies to the resistor ratio that sets G and to mismatch between the two devices generating ΔV_BE. Mismatch standard deviation falls as one over the square root of device area, so the only real lever is size: the 2022 design cited below occupies 0.103 square millimetres, about 382 by 270 micrometres, for a circuit containing a handful of devices.

There is also a structural trap. The loop equation that sets the operating current has a second solution at zero current, where every branch is off and everything is self-consistent, so a bandgap needs a start-up circuit whose only job is to push it out of that state and then stay out of the way.

sections.heading: Below one volt, and without a bipolar transistor
sections.body_md: The 1.2-volt answer became a problem once supplies dropped below it. The way out is to stop adding voltages and start adding currents: generate a PTAT current and a CTAT current, sum them into a resistor, and the output is whatever that resistor says — any fraction of the bandgap you like, with the same first-order cancellation. A 90-nanometre design reported in 2025 takes this to an extreme, running low-threshold MOSFETs in subthreshold, where drain current is exponential in gate voltage just as a bipolar's collector current is exponential in V_BE, and summing CTAT, PTAT and a curvature-correction current. It reports 205 millivolts of output from a 0.5-volt supply at 16.28 ppm/°C over −40 to 130 °C, drawing 0.67 microwatts, with 1.65 percent per volt line sensitivity and −50 decibels of supply rejection at 10 kilohertz. Note what the low-voltage, low-power version gives up: its temperature coefficient is roughly six times the trimmed bipolar design's.

glossary.definition: The forward voltage across a bipolar transistor's base-emitter junction at a given current — near 650 mV in silicon at room temperature. It is the most reproducible absolute voltage a chip can make, and it drifts about −2 mV/K.
25.85 mV at 300 K. It sets the scale of every exponential current-voltage relationship in a semiconductor, and its slope with temperature, k/q = 0.0862 mV/K, is a pure constant with no process in it.

Proportional to absolute temperature, and complementary to it. These are the two opposite-sign temperature behaviours a reference adds together: the first comes from a difference of junction voltages, the second from a junction voltage itself.

The fractional change in output per degree, in parts per million. It is normally quoted as the total output spread over a stated temperature range divided by the nominal voltage and by that range — so the range is part of the number and two quoted figures are not comparable without it.

The temperature dependence left after the linear term has been cancelled. It comes from the V_T·ln(T) term in the base-emitter voltage, and it is why a first-order reference stalls somewhere around 13 ppm/°C.
The 1974 self-biased bandgap topology used in the AD580, which added on-chip buffering so the reference could drive a load and be scaled to standard outputs such as 2.5 V and 5 V.

foundations.try_this: Bias one small-signal NPN — a 2N3904 is fine — at 100 µA and record V_BE, then at 1 mA and record it again. The difference should be (kT/q)·ln(10) = 59.5 mV at room temperature. Now tape a thermocouple to the package, warm it with a hot-air gun in 10 °C steps up to about 70 °C, and plot both V_BE and ΔV_BE against temperature. V_BE should fall at roughly 2 mV/K and ΔV_BE should rise at (k/q)·ln(10) = 0.198 mV/K. If your ΔV_BE slope is off, your two currents are not in the ratio you think they are — which is exactly why a real reference uses a current mirror rather than a bench supply. Then read Section 2 of the Micromachines paper below and work out which term of its V_EB(T) model a two-point measurement cannot see.
